questions.q: In the TokenBlockDataset, how is the target sequence `y` related to the input sequence `x`?
options: y is a random permutation of x
y is x shifted one position to the right -- the next token at each position
y is the reverse of x
y is identical to x
questions.explain: Each example slices a block_size+1 chunk of token IDs: the first block_size tokens are the input x, and the same chunk shifted one position is the target y, so the model learns to predict the next token at every position.

questions.q: Why does the training loop call `logits.view(-1, vocab_size)` and `y.view(-1)` before computing cross-entropy loss?
options: To convert the tensors to a different dtype
Because F.cross_entropy expects (N, num_classes) logits and (N,) integer targets, not the model's native (batch, block_size, vocab_size) shape
To reduce GPU memory usage
Because the model only outputs one token at a time
questions.explain: The model outputs logits shaped (batch, block_size, vocab_size). F.cross_entropy needs them flattened to (N, vocab_size) with matching (N,) targets, so both tensors are reshaped with .view(-1, ...) before the loss call.

questions.q: What does torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ do in this training loop, and why include it for a model this small?
options: It removes dropout layers during evaluation
It rescales gradients so their norm doesn't exceed a threshold, guarding against loss spikes even in a small model
It increases the learning rate automatically
It is only needed when using mixed precision, never otherwise
questions.explain: Gradient clipping caps the gradient norm before the optimizer step. Even a tiny model trained from scratch can hit sharp loss spikes early in training, and clipping keeps those spikes from derailing the run.

questions.q: What is the purpose of gradient accumulation, as used in the optional Chapter 7 block?
options: It permanently changes the model architecture
It simulates a larger effective batch size by summing gradients across several mini-batches before stepping the optimizer
It replaces the need for a learning-rate schedule
It converts the model to run on CPU only
questions.explain: Gradient accumulation backpropagates over several mini-batches, scaling and summing their gradients, and only calls optimizer.step() every accum_steps batches — giving an effective batch size of batch_size times accum_steps without needing that much memory at once.

questions.q: Why does the guide recommend checkpointing even for a training run that only takes about 20 minutes?
options: Checkpointing is required by PyTorch and cannot be skipped
So you can resume or roll back to a saved state instead of re-running training from scratch, and so Lesson 59 has a saved model to evaluate
Checkpoints make the model train faster
Checkpointing is only useful for models larger than one billion parameters
questions.explain: Even a short run is worth saving: a checkpoint lets you resume, roll back to your best validation loss, or avoid retraining from scratch -- and Lesson 59's evaluation step loads this exact checkpoint.
